gate: You read the tide marks on the wall and count the hours before the hall floods.
You deduce which of the seven doors is real from the salt dried on its sill.
Waist deep in the black cellar, you navigate by the pull of the cold current.
You rig the rusted pulley so the gate rises without a hand on the chain.
You recall the verse the drowned choir sang and answer the lock in its tongue.
You read the runes worn into the anchor stone by centuries of chain.
You deduce the weight of the sunk bell from the groan of its rusted beam.
You navigate the bone corridors by the salt crust that thickens toward the sea.
Into the cistern wall you rig a pipe of old bone and the cold water drains away.
One flagstone in the hall rings hollow under the heel and you name it before you cross.
You read the scratches a drowned hand left on the cell door, counting the tides.
You deduce from the rust where the water once stood, and where it will stand again.
You navigate the black lake by the echo of a dropped bone.
You rig the sunk ship's bell rope to ring when the choir comes near.
You recall the map you saw drawn in salt, now washed from the stone.
A drowned sailor's rope is knotted in fives and you read the depth he was working at.
You deduce the lock's answer from the teeth missing in a rusted key.
You navigate the dark by the cold of the salt walls on your left palm.
You rig a bone lever under the gate stone and wait for the tide to do the lifting.
The stair has no bottom in the lamplight and you know the count of it from an old chart.
You count the drips from the arch and know how long the ceiling has left.
You work out which lever drains the hall from the rust stains under each.
You follow the draught through the ossuary to a door hidden behind the skulls.
You notice that the rats all run one way and follow them toward the dry air.
You judge the depth of the flooded stair by the color of the water on each step.
You match the key to its lock by the shape of the rust it left on the hook.
You notice the choir only sings when the tide turns and time your crossing to it.
You map the drowned streets by the bells that still ring under the water.
You spot the trap in the corridor floor from the dust that has not settled on one tile.
You set the broken salt dial by the drip and the door beneath it opens.
You work out the combination of the bone lock from the verses cut above it.
You reckon the weight the rope bridge will hold from the knots its builders tied.
You listen to the water in the pipes and find the one that runs toward the air.
You turn the drowned compass until its needle stops arguing with the current.
You read the ship's log by lantern and learn where the captain hid the hatch key.
You match the floor tiles to the painted ceiling and step only on the stars.
You count the steps of the guard that walks above and cross between them.
You learn the lantern oil will last forty breaths and choose the shorter tunnel.
You notice the statue's hand points at the wrong hour and set it right.
You solve the riddle carved on the ferry post before the ferryman asks it twice.
chain: Along the ossuary shelf you read the names cut in bone and turn the skull set wrong.
The lantern flame leans to one crack, so you deduce a shaft and follow the draft up.
The bell tolls twice and you recall that the second toll means water, then climb.
Down the flooded well you lower the lantern on its chain and read the floor it lights.
By the wall chain you navigate the flooded hall and stop where the links go under.
Out of a rotted door you rig a raft and pole it over the black water to the far ledge.
Of the two chains at the wreck you deduce which still holds and cross on it.
When the hall fills you recall which way the water ran and take the stair against it.
You read the warning cut above the door, then choose the passage it does not name.
You read the frost on the grates, then go down the one where the air is warm.
You find the pressure plate by the bones heaped on it, then wedge it with a stone.
You trace the current to the drain, then follow the drain to the open sea air.
You decode the lock's first ring, then the second, from the wear on the brass.
You notice the rust is fresher on one bolt, then turn that bolt and not the others.
You work out the ferry's times from its rope burns, then wait for the empty crossing.
You match the burial niche to the name on the key, then open it without a sound.
You notice the draught turns cold, then turn back before the air runs out.
You chart the cellars in chalk, then follow your own marks out when the lantern fails.
You learn the swing of the hanging blades, then walk through on the counted beat.
You find the true stair in the mirror hall, then close your eyes to climb it.
You rig the fallen pulley to the portcullis, then hang your weight on the far rope.
You spot which pipe feeds the flood, then plug it with a boot and a strip of sail.
You guess the watchword from the choir's hymn, then speak it at the iron grille.
You read the depth marks on the pier, then time the dash across the mud flat.
You sort the bones on the scale by weight, then set the last one and hear the lock turn.
You recall the order of the drowned bells, then ring them in it with a thrown stone.
You trace the faint writing in the silt, then brush away the rest to read the date.
You catch the wrong echo in the hall, then find the false wall that threw it.
You tally the doors you have passed, then realise the corridor has been bending back.
You weigh the lantern oil against the map, then take the passage that ends sooner.
You work the stuck astrolabe free of salt, then set it to the star painted overhead.
You find the hidden hinge in the ossuary wall, then push the panel where it gives.
You mark the water rising a hand an hour, then plan the climb with time to spare.
You spot the one lamp wick still trimmed, then follow the path its keeper takes.
You unpick the knot code on the rope, then pull the strand that opens the trap.
You test each rung for rot by its sound, then climb only on the ones that ring true.
You piece the broken tablet back together, then read the name the door wants.
You measure the gap with the lantern chain, then cut a plank to span it.
You smell lamp oil somewhere in the dark, then find the store of it by the wall.
You follow the gulls' bones to the old nest, then find the air shaft above it.
